extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, and examiners assessing witness testimony / forensic practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing the reliability of witness sensory perception, memory, and imaginative reconstruction in legal examinations; covers perception-to-recognition transition, sensory limitations, expert witness bias, suggestion, orientation, and indicators of certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and nature of pain perception in wounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripheral pain is perceived with a delay (about a third of a second after the cause); wounded persons often sense stabs, shots, and blows as pushes rather than immediate penetrating pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victims commonly report only a 'hard push' rather than the cold or penetration of a blade; the person who inflicted the wound often feels the entrance more clearly (sensation concentrated in the right thumb at the hilt). Use this to distinguish which assailant inflicted a given wound; when the victim is explained the physiological facts his testimony may become more honest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition/misalocalization of cutaneous sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of skin displaced (e.g., skin covering a bone pulled over a fleshy part) 'can not easily identify the point of stimulation'; vigorous twists and certain postures cause frequent transpositions making localization of a blow or stab very hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the body is twisted or the skin is pulled aside (e.g., arm held backward), localization of a wound is unreliable. Examiners should note posture/skin displacement at time of injury and treat localization testimony cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion between wetness and cold/smooth surfaces (blood misidentification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensation of wetness is composed of that of cold and easy movement over surface; touching a cold smooth metal may be taken for wetness and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses and companions may mistake metal for blood or vice versa; mistakes about whether there was bleeding have led to frequent confusion—do not take immediate statements of 'I felt blood' at face value without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of repetition on tactile perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (summation) intensifies and clarifies the sensation of touch; repeated stroking or holding gives clearer perception than a single touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing facts by touch (or evaluating tactile testimony), ask whether touches were single or repeated—repetition can reveal essential differences that a single touch misses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty determining shape/form by touch
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very difficult to determine merely by touch whether a thing is straight or crooked, flat, convex or concave; experiments show directional pressure changes can produce illusions of convexity/concavity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat tactile claims about shape/form skeptically. The method of touching (pressure and movement) can create systematic illusions (Weber experiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion over skin alters perceived speed and may cause errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion of a point at a constant rate over a sizable piece of skin can give the impression of increasing rapidity in one direction (Vierordt); direction and extent of skin covered affect definiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes may occur in describing cuts, scratches, and similar wounds because perceived speed/direction can be distorted by skin-area effects; consider direction and area when evaluating such testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in pressure sensitivity across the body (Weber/Fechner findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensation of weight differs greatly across skin regions; e.g., to notice removal of coins requires different numbers at different sites (one dollar from top of finger; five dollars from abdomen, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known sensitivity differences (forehead, temples, eyelids, inside forearm = most sensitive; lips, trunk, fingernails = least) to evaluate claims about feeling pressure/weight—useful in assault/choking cases. The text gives a specific list of coin-removal thresholds for body sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition vs. perception and the problem of reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition indicates only that an object has sufficiently impressed a mind to keep it known and identifiable; modern psychology does not see sharp boundaries between perception and memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawyers must consider whether a witness can later reproduce an object or event. Distinguish between simple sensory apprehension and recognition that allows identification over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes in observation: oversight vs. wrong observation; role of preconceived opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors are classified as positive (wrong observation) or negative (oversight). Oversights occur largely through preconceived opinions which cause people to accept exceptions without testing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test claimed exceptions experimentally where possible; be wary of conclusions based on untested assumptions. Example: historical errors by Copernicus opponents or the spider-web/arson plausibility check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of prior conceptions ('perceptual capital' / memory-images) on testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: People conceive new information by attaching it to images and 'perceptual capital' they already possess; completeness of earlier conceptions determines how accurately a new thing can be conceived and described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating testimony, identify what prior images or experiences the witness brought to the event. Failure to account for differing perceptual capital produces incompatible descriptions; examiners should adapt their questions to the witness's image-base without introducing incorrect comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and danger of comparisons and analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners often use comparisons presupposing shared experience; but everyone takes comparisons from his own experience—comparisons are intelligible only if the witness has had a like experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid or qualify analogies unless you are confident the witness shares the reference frame; with peasants or specialized populations, first understand their life/imagery before using powerful comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of attention and the unreliability of obvious detail perception
rubrics_metrics.description: People often fail to perceive salient details even when in their field of perception—the more foolish and obvious a trick, the more certain it is to succeed; simple demonstrations show how little detail observers recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-expect detailed recall from witnesses; probing or shaming prompts ('But you will know') may elicit answers but not reliable information. Use careful, non-suggestive methods to elicit what was actually perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subconscious ('dark') perceptions and their effect on testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: A great part of intelligence depends on 'dark perceptions' rising into consciousness; more intelligent witnesses often have more useful subconscious perceptions that can be formed into explicit testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing testimonies, be aware that differences may stem from varying degrees of subconscious elaboration rather than dishonesty. Help can sometimes draw out subconscious perceptions, but assistance risks suggestion; take testimony as given and later test for alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witnesses: stronger attention but one-sided apprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts perceive their specialty with vigorous attention but their apprehension is often one-sided and professionally colored; they may overlook legally important aspects outside their interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume experts are the best witnesses for all factual matters. Expect oversight of legally important details when an expert focuses on technical aspects (examples: doctor distracted by surgical concern; cabinet-maker focused on wood rather than how a drawer was forced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation and localization specialties affect testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: People differ in their sense of orientation/localization; those who orient well will give testimony framed around place/direction, while others may lack such spatial impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a witness has a sense of local orientation (and how it shapes their perceptions); use this specialty to elicit reliable spatial information and beware of witnesses for whom orientation is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time required for apprehension and speech rate as indicator of certainty (Cattell)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time to identify a single letter is about 1/4 second; pronunciation about 1/10 second; better knowledge of language allows faster repetition. More definite conception leads to faster reproduction; rapidity of speech may indicate how certain and practiced a witness is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speech rate and hesitations as heuristic indicators: slow, hesitant speech may signal uncertainty or conscious reconstruction; rapid, fluent speech may indicate conviction or rehearsed memory. But account for individual idiosyncrasies and language familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of imagination and substitutional adequacy of mental images
rubrics_metrics.description: Things witnesses tell us often existed previously in imagination; the representative value of images varies with how well the subject is known (e.g., one's own dog vs. historical dogs known only by description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the origin and basis of a witness's images (direct perception, pictures, hearsay, or pure invention). The more remote or second-hand the basis, the less reliable the descriptive testimony. Remember representation cannot be identical to the object (limitations noted by Helmholtz).
